sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

content.text:
Case L09: segment the lipomatous soft-tissue tumor on this T1-weighted MRI.

Volume: 250x250x331 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

case L09 | sequence T1 | shape (i,j,k)=(250, 250, 331) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: lipomatous soft-tissue tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).

At slice 196, I spot a heterogeneous mass with intermediate signal mixed into the bright fat — this looks like a lipomatous tumor spanning roughly axial 92-231, possibly extending through the sartorius canal and encircling the femoral vessels. The mixed signal intensity raises the possibility this is an atypical lipomatous tumor rather than a simple lipoma, so I want to look more closely at slice 196 with annotations.

I'm examining a lipomatous mass with a thin capsule that seems to surround or displace the gracilis and adductor muscles, tracing how the capsule boundary curves around the fat region between the muscles, which appears slightly grayer than the subcutaneous fat.

This is likely the deep fascia (fascia lata) separating subcutaneous fat from the thigh muscles, with the lipoma actually sitting as intermuscular fat between sartorius, gracilis, and the adductors inside that fascial boundary. I'll place positive points at the two fat regions near the muscle crescent and see how the model segments it.

That 508 mL segmentation seems too large, likely capturing the whole medial muscle compartment rather than just the tumor capsule — I'm wondering if the outline is actually tracing the sartorius, gracilis, and adductor muscles along with the fat, since those muscles still look relatively normal in density on closer inspection of the axial slices.

In lipomatous tumor datasets like WORC's Lipo set, ground truth typically marks only the fatty mass itself, so if this lesion is intermuscular rather than intramuscular, the segmentation should exclude muscle tissue entirely — but the large fat region with femoral vessels running through it at axial 139 makes me uncertain whether that's tumor engulfing the vessels or just unusually prominent adductor canal fat given this patient's overall adiposity. I want to cross-reference this with the sagittal view, where there's a bright oval fatty mass with slightly gray signal in the posterior-mid thigh that could help clarify the tumor's true extent.

Looking again at the sagittal images, the posterior-distal thigh region near the popliteal fossa shows heterogeneous grayish areas, but that could just be normal popliteal fat rather than pathology, so I'm reconsidering and checking the axial slice for a heterogeneous bright mass instead.

I'm trying to triangulate the gray-tinged mass seen in both axial and sagittal views by converting display pixel coordinates into actual slice indices, estimating it spans roughly axial slices 118-215 in a posterior-medial position between the thigh muscles. To confirm this location more precisely, I should pull up sagittal slice 125 with annotation marks for clarity.

At sagittal slice 128, I'm examining a large fatty region extending from the popliteal area up toward slice 220, noting an oval mass with slightly grayer signal than surrounding muscle that could be either normal popliteal fat or a fatty tumor — I need to determine which it is.

This is tricky since a lipoma can be nearly isointense with normal fat, and the mass seems to be displacing muscles in axial view 139, suggesting the medial intermuscular fat compartment is abnormally enlarged from roughly axial 60 to 230. I think my earlier segmentation mistakenly captured the entire muscle compartment rather than just the fat, so I should restart with a box or lasso selection targeting the fatty region specifically, refining it with negative points placed on muscle, and first re-examine the axial anatomy at slice 139 with the mask outline overlaid.

content.text: axial 150/331 | crop mask | marks fine | overlay outline | v1 | tool calls 9/40, prompts 1/15

content.thinking:
I'm tracing a thin curved fascia line in the fatty region between muscles, which seems to encircle an oval area that could represent the lipoma with its capsule.

The grayer fat region bounded by muscles near the femoral vessels looks like the likely lipoma site, but the mask is probably including too much surrounding muscle. Excluding every individual muscle (sartorius, gracilis, adductor magnus) with negative points across all slices seems impractical, so I'm considering whether an intensity-based candidate selection might better isolate the fat mass instead.

Actually, I think a cleaner approach is to checkout v0 to reset the mask, then lasso the fat region in just one axial slice and let the model propagate in 3D rather than adding negative points everywhere. Before doing that though, I want to pin down the lesion's location more precisely — scanning across slices 109 through 231, I'm noting where the fat/muscle boundary looks like a discrete heterogeneous mass with a capsule (clearest around slice 196, posteromedial) versus where it's just normal adductor canal fat around the vessels, and I'm also checking the coronal view for an elongated fatty region running through the medial thigh between muscles.

My working theory is that this is a large intermuscular lipoma in the medial thigh encasing the femoral vessels, so the ground truth mask likely covers the fat (and maybe the vessels) but excludes the surrounding muscles. My plan is to checkout v0 and place a lasso on the fat region at axial slice 150, carefully excluding the muscle bodies, then evaluate the resulting mask. Alternatively, I could try negative points directly on the muscle labels in the current mask — at slice 150 there seem to be a few distinct muscle components (sartorius, gracilis, and a larger one like semimembranosus or adductor magnus) — and see if three negative points removes them cleanly in 3D.

I need to figure out whether this represents the actual lesion or just normal intermuscular fat following the adductor canal and femoral vessels.

A lipoma would typically appear as a discrete mass, not this long narrow strip, which makes me question my identification. The dimensions don't quite match between the coronal (15-20mm wide) and axial (30x40mm) views either, so I want to revisit axial 196, which showed a discrete heterogeneous gray mass that might be the actual lesion, along with that darker oval I noted on sagittal 125 — I should look more closely at axial 200 to clarify this.

content.text: axial 200/331 | crop mask | marks fine | overlay outline | v2 | tool calls 13/40, prompts 2/15

content.thinking:
At axial slice 200, I'm noting a rounded region with heterogeneous gray signal inside a capsule-like ring, surrounded by fat. There's a well-defined oval area of grayer tissue bordered by a thin bright rim in the lower fat region that could represent the mass, along with a larger curved fascial line enclosing the area.

I'm now considering the muscles on the left within this fascial ring and the fat pockets between them and the ring. My suspicion is that the oval heterogeneous region is the actual lesion, with the broader fatty area representing a lipomatous tumor and the oval being a more atypical component — consistent with what the sagittal view showed earlier. To pin down the anatomic level, I'm estimating this axial slice sits roughly 100mm below the femoral head, placing it in the proximal third of the thigh where I'd expect to see sartorius, adductor longus, gracilis, adductor magnus, and the femoral vessels medially.

I'm now reasoning about whether the tumor is actually an intermuscular lipomatous mass spanning the whole fatty region inside the fascia lata, not just the oval — which would mean the posterior fat pocket currently excluded from the mask should actually be included, though it's hard to tell if that's tumor or just normal fat. Trying to estimate the oval's volume from its dimensions across slices, I get something like 50-70 mL, but I want to cross-check this by looking more carefully at the mask overlay in the sagittal views again.

Looking again at the oval's gray-tinged mass with a thin dark capsule rim on its posterior edge, bordered below by bright fat with irregular dark streaks that could be vessels, I'm wondering if this heterogeneous oval represents an atypical lipomatous tumor rather than a simple lipoma, since lipomas are typically homogeneous and fat-isointense. I want to trace the capsule across axial slices and check a coronal view through the oval's center to better understand its shape and boundaries.

Converting that display x of 113 to a sagittal index, I'm wondering if the display is mirrored, since the mask extent of 106-172 puts the oval's actual center closer to sagittal 128, not 113 — so there may be a left-right flip I need to account for.

I should pull up coronal slice 135 with the outline overlaid to actually see where the oval sits.

My working hypothesis is that the lesion is this large fat/gray mass in the medial thigh, and the current mask seems to partially capture it, though I'm still unsure whether adjacent fat pockets outside the fascia, the distal popliteal region, and the thin posterior strip near the sciatic nerve should also be included. Based on femur position relative to center, I'm concluding this is likely a left thigh with display left as medial, so the muscle group at that location is sartorius/gracilis/adductors. That points toward the lesion being an intermuscular fatty mass located in the medial thigh compartment.

The gray heterogeneous tissue between muscle bundles near that same region seems to be captured by the current mask outline. I should also check whether the mask correctly extends through the upper thigh and down into the popliteal fossa, since normal popliteal fat usually isn't part of the tumor unless there's direct extension, and some slices show the fat continuing smoothly toward the knee joint alongside the popliteal vessels.

Let me examine the sagittal view with the outline overlay to trace the overall shape of the lesion from top to bottom.

I recall similar fat regions with vessels in the medial thigh at nearby axial levels, but I'm still not confident enough in this mapping to call it definitive — I should check the segmentation more carefully.

Given lipomas near the adductor canal often extend along the neurovascular bundle into the popliteal fossa, and the fat here is contiguous without a clear contrast boundary, I'm leaning toward annotators having outlined the mass by its capsule rather than by fat signal alone. I want to check the axial views around slice 100 and 70 to look for a capsule boundary that separates tumor from normal fat.

I saved a mask for case L09, but I have low confidence that it matches the tumor's true extent.

**What the mask covers:** about 229 mL of fatty tissue between the muscles of the medial and posterior thigh. It runs from near the knee (axial slice 35) to the upper thigh (axial slice 248) and surrounds the femoral vessels. Near the top end, around axial slices 180–212, it includes a rounded area that looks more grey and uneven than ordinary fat.

**How it got there:** My first two points on the fat at axial slice 190 made the model take the whole medial muscle compartment, muscles included (508 mL). Four negative points on the muscles brought it down to the fat only. Filling holes changed nothing, and I rejected all three automatic suggestions because they were subcutaneous fat or muscle. In total I used 23 of 40 tool calls and 2 of 15 model prompts.

**Why confidence is low:**
- **Unclear border with normal fat.** On this T1 scan the tumor's fat looks the same as normal fat, and I couldn't find a clear capsule along most of its length. The lower part of the mask, in the fat behind the knee, may be normal fat rather than tumor.
- **Some uneven tissue may be missed.** At axial slice 212, part of the uneven fatty tissue lies outside the mask. A small darker patch near the top (seen on sagittal slices 134–139) is left as an unfilled hole.
- **Possibly the wrong structure.** The tumor might only be the smaller grey oval near axial slice 200 rather than the whole fatty region. If so, the mask is much too large.

The mask also has a second, negligible fragment (under 0.1 mL) that I didn't remove.
